strengths: The paper addresses important perceptual aspects of UV unwrapping (semantic chart alignment and seam visibility/occlusion) that are often overlooked by purely distortion-minimizing geometric methods.

Formulating seam extraction differentiably using a soft-max over local UV distances to enable backpropagation of an ambient occlusion (AO) loss is a creative and neat integration with neural parameterization backbones.
The qualitative visualizations (e.g., checkerboard rendering and seam distributions) clearly illustrate the benefit of steering cuts into occluded regions.
Extensive comparisons are provided against both classical/industrial tools (Blender, Maya, xatlas, OptCuts) and recent learning-based methods (FlexPara).
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the semantic-aware pipeline is quite limited: it relies on an off-the-shelf geometric segmentation (classical Shape Diameter Function with GMM and graph cuts) as an offline pre-processing step, fits the base neural parameterizer independently per part, and places them into a naive uniform grid. Framing this modular heuristic pipeline as 'unsupervised representation learning for semantic parameterization' overstates the algorithmic contribution.

The UV packing strategy (a uniform G x G regular grid) is rudimentary. It leads to substantial wasted UV space and poor packing efficiency compared to standard industrial pack solvers, yet UV domain utilization is not quantitatively evaluated.

The quantitative evaluation of semantic awareness in Table 2 uses SAMesh predictions as pseudo-ground truth, which is problematic since SAMesh is an unverified zero-shot heuristic partitioner rather than annotated ground truth.

There is an apparent trade-off where the proposed method exhibits noticeably lower geometric fidelity (equiareality/conformality) compared to traditional optimization methods like OptCuts (e.g., equiareality of ~0.61 vs 0.89).

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addressing seam visibility and semantic part coherence directly tackles key practical bottlenecks in texture generation and 3D asset workflows.

Differentiable formulation for seam visibility: The derivation of a smooth, differentiable soft seam membership score based on UV neighborhood distances combined with ambient occlusion (AO) is intuitive, effective, and readily integrable into gradient-based parameterization pipelines.

Convincing visual results: Rendered textured models and checkerboard visualizations demonstrate that the visibility-aware objective successfully steers seams into occluded/inconspicuous areas, resulting in fewer perceptual artifacts compared to baselines like FlexPara and OptCuts.

Comprehensive presentation and documentation: The appendix provides extensive qualitative comparisons across multiple viewpoints and detailed descriptions of network architectures and loss formulations.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the 'semantic-aware' pipeline: The semantic partitioning is essentially an offline, classical pre-processing step using the Shape Diameter Function (ShDF, Shapira et al., 2008), GMM fitting, and alpha-expansion graph-cuts. The neural network does not learn semantic representations across shapes; it simply optimizes independent instances of an existing parameterizer (FlexPara backbone) on each pre-extracted submesh.

Naive UV atlas packing: Packing the per-part charts into a rigid G x G regular grid with identical scale factors simplifies the implementation but leads to poor UV space utilization (significant wasted texture space) and unequal texel resolution across parts of varying surface areas.

Evaluation on semantic metrics is skewed: Comparing semantic segmentation metrics (Hamming Distance and Rand Index against SAMesh) with general-purpose UV unwrapping tools (xatlas, Blender SmartUV, Maya) is somewhat unfair, as traditional tools segment charts purely to minimize geometric distortion rather than to identify semantic parts.

Trade-off in geometric distortion: Quantitative results in Table 1 and Table 2 indicate that the proposed method suffers from lower equiareality (area preservation) and lower conformality compared to established tools like xatlas and OptCuts, reflecting a noticeable penalty in distortion to accommodate the visibility and part-partitioning objectives.

Limited benchmark size: Quantitative evaluation appears to be conducted on a relatively small set of meshes (e.g., Duckie, Cow, Fish, Rabbit) rather than a standardized large-scale benchmark (e.g., Thingi10K subsets commonly used in modern UV mapping literature).

strengths: Relevant and practical problem setting: addressing seam visibility and semantic structure in UV parameterization is an important challenge for automated 3D content generation.
Formulating a soft, differentiable proxy for seam detection (using LogSumExp and sigmoid over UV neighbor distances) enables backpropagating view-exposure/ambient occlusion losses.
Extensive visual comparisons against both industry/open-source tools (Autodesk Maya, Blender, xatlas) and recent state-of-the-art methods (OptCuts, FlexPara).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed framework largely combines existing components. The semantic-aware pipeline relies on a classical off-the-shelf geometric segmentation technique (Shape Diameter Function + GMM + Graph Cut from Shapira et al., 2008), after which the existing FlexPara/Parapoint backbone is simply trained independently per part. The visibility-aware component is a straightforward addition of an ambient occlusion loss over the differentiable seam formulation adapted from Zhao et al. (2025).

Unconvincing integration of semantic and visibility objectives: While the paper presents the method as a unified framework addressing both objectives simultaneously, the two modules operate mostly disjointly (partition-and-parameterize vs. global seam-AO loss). The paper provides minimal explanation of how both are jointly trained when combined ('Ours - Semantic+Visibility-Aware Param'), and Table 1/2 shows degradation across several metrics when both are enabled.

Flawed evaluation methodology for semantic awareness: In Table 2, semantic awareness is evaluated against SAMesh outputs treated as ground truth. Comparing UV atlases from geometric unwrappers (which optimize developability rather than object semantic parts) against a part-segmentation mask naturally favors a pipeline that explicitly segments the mesh by parts first. This does not genuinely validate whether the UV parameterization itself facilitates cross-shape consistency or semantic transfer.

Absence of quantitative downstream validation: Despite repeatedly motivating the work by downstream 3D texture synthesis and editing workflows, the paper contains no downstream experiments (such as text-to-texture generation quality, cross-mesh texture transfer, or user studies). Only basic checkerboard visualizations are provided.

Degradation in geometric distortion and poor atlas packing: Adding the visibility objective leads to a noticeable drop in equiareality (from 0.8934 in OptCuts to 0.6093 in Ours). Furthermore, the semantic atlas aggregation relies on a naive regular grid placement that causes significant UV space wastage, yet standard UV metrics such as chart area utilization / packing efficiency are omitted.

Small-scale experimental evaluation: The quantitative and qualitative evaluations are performed on only a small handful of isolated shapes (e.g., Rabbit, Cow, Fish, Duckie) rather than standard large-scale benchmarks (e.g., ShapeNet, Thingi10K, or Objaverse).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in 3D content creation: UV parameterization that considers both semantic organization and seam visibility rather than purely geometric distortion.
The formulation of the differentiable seam extraction and ambient occlusion (AO) weighted loss provides an effective and differentiable mechanism to steer seams toward visually occluded areas.

Conducts an extensive user preference study with 115 participants (including 45 domain professionals and 3D artists), showing strong perceptual preference for the proposed seam placement and semantic organization.
Provides thorough qualitative comparisons and ablation studies evaluating different segmenters (ShDF, SAMesh, PartField) and packing strategies.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in the semantic-aware module: The semantic-aware pipeline is largely a disjoint multi-stage heuristic—it runs off-the-shelf 3D segmentation (e.g., ShDF or SAMesh), optimizes an existing neural parameterization backbone (FlexPara) independently on each disconnected sub-mesh, and places them into a basic regular grid. There is no joint end-to-end semantic learning.

Significant trade-off in geometric distortion: The quantitative results in Tables 1 and 3 demonstrate a substantial drop in equiareality (area preservation drops from ~0.89 in OptCuts and ~0.90 in Blender to ~0.61–0.67 in the proposed method), which is a critical metric for texture stretching in production workflows.

Severe training computation overhead for the visibility-aware pipeline: As shown in Table 9, the per-mesh training time of the visibility-aware model averages over 8.6 hours (~31,160 seconds) compared to ~21 minutes (~1,285 seconds) for FlexPara, driven by the expensive per-iteration neighborhood checks in UV space. This severely hinders its practicality in standard asset pipelines.

Lack of evaluation on actual generative downstream tasks: Although modern generative texture synthesis is cited as the primary motivation in the introduction and abstract, the experimental validation relies almost entirely on checkerboard patterns and color assignments, without demonstrating actual text-to-texture or image-to-texture generation pipelines.

strengths: Addresses key practical limitations in automated and learning-based UV parameterization by explicitly targeting semantic chart consistency and visual seam concealment rather than solely minimizing geometric distortion.

The visibility-aware objective is neatly formulated with a soft, differentiable seam-detection mechanism in UV space coupled with ambient occlusion (AO) weighting, successfully steering seams to occluded regions.

Comprehensive empirical validation, including qualitative texturing comparisons (e.g., checkerboard continuity), quantitative geometric/perceptual metrics, and an unusually thorough user study involving 115 participants (including 45 graphics and media industry professionals).
Detailed ablation studies examining alternative 3D segmentation methods (ShDF, SAMesh, PartField) and commercial UV packing pipelines (Maya, Blender, Houdini).
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the semantic-aware pipeline is relatively modular and incremental: it relies on standard off-the-shelf 3D segmentation (ShDF or foundation models) as a decoupled pre-processing step, independently running the baseline neural parameterizer on each component and then applying a packing heuristic, rather than learning joint semantic-geometric representations.

Significant computational overhead during training for the visibility-aware branch: Table 9 shows that training times increase from ~20 minutes for FlexPara to ~8.6 hours on average due to repeated per-iteration k-NN distance evaluations in UV space.

Noticeable degradation in area preservation (equiareality): As reported in Tables 1 and 7, introducing the visibility-aware seam objective drops equiareality from 0.893 (OptCuts) and 0.676 (FlexPara) down to 0.609 (and 0.637 for the combined variant), highlighting a non-trivial trade-off between seam concealment and local area stretch.

Evaluating semantic awareness quantitatively against SAMesh as a pseudo ground truth introduces ambiguity, especially given the ablation discussion noting that SAMesh itself occasionally fails to capture fine structural parts compared to other segmenters.

strengths: Addresses two critical and perceptually meaningful bottlenecks in automated UV unwrapping: placing seams in visually inconspicuous areas and structuring UV charts according to semantic parts.

The differentiable visibility-aware loss leveraging pre-computed ambient occlusion (AO) and soft seam detection provides an intuitive and effective mechanism to guide seam placement towards occluded crevices and under-surfaces.

The paper includes a thorough user study with 115 participants (including 45 industry practitioners such as UV/layout and modeling artists), providing strong perceptual validation for the visual quality of the resulting parameterizations.

Extensive qualitative visualizations, checkerboard texture comparisons, and comparisons against both modern neural baselines (FlexPara) and traditional/commercial industry tools (OptCuts, Blender, Maya, xatlas).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The base parameterization network and differentiable seam detection formulation are largely inherited directly from FlexPara (Zhao et al., 2025). The semantic-aware module is an engineering pipeline combining classical segmentation (ShDF + graph cuts) with per-part independent optimization, rather than an integrated end-to-end representation learning framework.

Prohibitive per-mesh training times: The visibility-aware optimization requires between 4.5 and 13 hours per mesh (averaging ~8.6 hours / 31,160s, as shown in Table 9), which is an order of magnitude slower than FlexPara (~21 minutes) and orders of magnitude slower than OptCuts (240 seconds). This severely limits its practical adoption in production pipelines.

Noticeable degradation in geometric distortion: Table 1 and Table 7 show that incorporating visibility and semantic objectives leads to a steep decline in area-preservation (equiareality drops from 0.89 in OptCuts and 0.68 in FlexPara down to 0.61 in the visibility-aware model).

Rudimentary atlas packing in the main pipeline: Packing per-part charts into a fixed uniform G x G grid leads to poor UV space utilization and suboptimal texel distribution compared to standard industrial bin-packing / UV island packing routines (even though post-processing packing is ablated in the appendix).
